claim: A uniform-swing-based probabilistic seat model, when fed the actual final two-party-preferred result (not polling), forecasts Australian federal Labor/Coalition seat totals to within an average of +/-2.0 to 2.5 seats across ten elections from 1993 to 2019.
stance_target: uniform swing is a fairly accurate seat-forecasting method when the aggregate result is known precisely
scope_conditions: Australian federal elections 1993-2019, isolating swing-translation error from polling error
quoted_support: If a uniform swing model is given the correct 2pp result ahead of time, it'll be able to get the seat totals for the major parties to within +/- 2 to 3 seats on average.

claim: Adjusting uniform swing for a candidate/incumbency effect (worth roughly 1 point of two-party-preferred vote for major-party incumbents) reduces average forecast error across 1993-2019 Australian elections from 2.7% to 2.4%, an 11% relative error reduction.
stance_target: candidate-level covariates materially improve uniform swing forecasts
quoted_support: On average, adjusting for candidate effects reduces the average 2pp error from 2.7% to 2.4%. While that might not sound like a lot, this amounts to an 11% reduction in the average error.

claim: Combining a district's two-party lean from the last two elections (weighted roughly 2:1 in favour of the more recent one) instead of relying on only the most recent election also reduces average forecast error from 2.7% to 2.4% in Australian federal elections, a similar-sized gain to candidate-effect adjustment.
stance_target: combining multiple past elections' baseline lean improves on single-prior-election uniform swing
quoted_support: combining two-party lean estimates from the last two elections, as opposed to simply using the last election result, appears to improve forecast error by a similar degree as adjusting for candidate effects.

claim: Applied to the 2018 South Australian state election, blending two-election lean history versus plain uniform swing reduced average absolute forecast error from 2.73 to 2.57 points, a smaller (5.9% relative) improvement than at the federal level, suggesting the multi-election-lean method may be less useful in smaller, noisier state electorates.
stance_target: generalizability of the multi-election-lean improvement across scales of election
scope_conditions: South Australian state election 2018, n=1 backtest
quoted_support: This is a similar improvement to what we found at the 2021 WA state election – a 0.16% reduction in the average error (or a relative 5.9% reduction in error size).

claim: A detailed methodology exists for estimating district-level vote shares from an election two redistributions prior using polling-place-level tally data, declaration/postal vote reallocation and distance-based splitting of boundary polling places -- directly analogous to constructing a bureau-de-vote crosswalk across French redistricting.
stance_target: how to reconstruct historical baseline vote shares under electoral-unit boundary changes
scope_conditions: Australian federal electorates, AEC Tally Room polling-place data
quoted_support: For polling places where voters came from different electoral divisions, a weighted average of the declaration vote gap was calculated using the % of voters from each electoral division.

claim: Uniform-swing-based models systematically misfire in electorates undergoing structural realignment rather than typical mean reversion; South Australian seats Colton, Hartley and Black each shifted sharply toward the Liberals in 2018 after decades of tracking the statewide vote, and the model cannot distinguish whether this represents a one-off idiosyncratic shock (expected to revert) or a permanent partisan realignment.
stance_target: swing models reliably distinguish transient shocks from durable partisan realignment at the district level
scope_conditions: South Australian state elections, districts Colton/Hartley/Black, 2014-2022
quoted_support: It's also worth noting that while our model expects these seats to be less Liberal-leaning on average than at the last election, there is still a very real chance that they will become more Liberal-leaning... there is still a very real chance...
numbers: 1 in 6 to 1 in 3 chance of continued rightward shift per seat
2 in 3 chance at least one of four seats shifts further right
